kept.spine: Nothing presses the town at present, and a place kept this ready is not worth the price of trying.
What is out in the country is known here and spoken of by nobody, and the town counts that as the walls doing their work.
faces: A drover says the town asks a man what he is bringing in and never what he met on the road.
The men who hold the ways in say the bar goes down at dusk and no one has ever argued the hour with them.
A priest of one of the parishes holds that the roads and the men on the wall are prayed for in one breath.
One of the aldermen says the hall hears about the toll and the water and never about the nights.
A night patrolman reckons the complaints come to the watch at the gate and stop there.
A woman at the long table says the talk here is all about who stands the nights, and none of it about what is out beyond the walls.
A soldier of the garrison holds that nobody from the town comes out to watch the garrison drill.
A warden of one of the guilds reckons the trades pay for the wall at the gate and the whole town counts the safety as its own.
A stallholder says the stalls go up in the square whatever is loose in the country.
A clerk of one of the courts says the courts hear what the town does to itself and nothing of what the country does to it.
The elders say the young stand the nights and the old say how they are stood.

kept.poolKey: Invasion & War: walls AND professional garrison
kept.spine: A stranger is stopped at the gate before he is let in, and what he is let into is a town that pays soldiers of its own.
faces: A gatekeeper says a stranger pays at the gate, and what the gate owes the hall is settled later and elsewhere.
A clerk in the hall holds that a stranger who pays at the gate has paid the town, whatever the men on the gate tell him.
A bailiff says a man who paid at the gate may argue it before the court, and a stranger as readily as a carter.
A traveller reckons a pack is opened at the gate here and nothing taken out of it but the toll.
An innkeeper says the town is asked what the soldiers cost and never asked whether it wants them.

kept.spine: The town keeps a court and no room to hold anybody in, and what the law here can take from a man is his money or his place in the town.
faces: One of the watch says a man taken up after dark is dealt with after dark, there being nowhere to put him until morning.
A clerk of the court says the court hears in daylight what the watch settled in the dark and is asked about none of it first.
A woman who keeps the hall books reckons the purse does not run to a room to hold men in and never has.
A trader come in for the fair says a short weight is answered with a sum, and the man who gave it is back behind the same stall the next day.
A parish warden holds that the parish has ground for a man once he is dead and the town has no room for him while he lives.
A journeyman says a sum comes out of a man's takings and is forgotten, and the mark it leaves on his work is not.
The drinkers of the district say a man with a house here pays and stays, and a man without one is put on the road.
A rider who stopped a night says there is nothing here to take from a man who owns nothing in the town, and the road is what is left to give him.
A man on one of the gates says the watch brings him a man and a direction and no reason for either.
A man who draws the wage says what comes at the town is the garrison's business and the men walked out of the gate are not.

kept.spine: The town can pay for a crisis out of what it already takes in, and nobody here doubts the purse.
faces: A secretary of the city's offices says the hall asks the trades for no more than the trades can carry.
The guild master says the carrying falls to the guilds and the asking never does.
The guilds' account is the likelier, the hall having a purse to defend and the guilds only a bill.
The guard captain says the rounds are kept by men who are owed for keeping them.
A serjeant on the wall says a cart bound for the grain store is never held at the gate, whatever else is.
A messenger off the road says the people who praise the town's full store are the people who complain of their pay.
A carter at one of the taverns says the watch drinks here on money it has not been paid yet.
The soldiers hold that a town which can be fed through a crisis and does not meet their wage in full has decided something. It has not said what.
The people who deal there say what the hall is owed comes out of the day's takings before anything of their own does.
A canon holds that the town keeps its word to the dead sooner than it keeps its word to the living.

kept.poolKey: Disasters & Famine: granary AND parish care only
kept.spine: The town keeps a full grain store and no house for the sick. Whoever tends a sick man here comes out of the church.
faces: A cathedral clerk says a stranger asks where the sick are kept and is given a name instead of a place.
A clerk of one of the markets says grain is easy to buy here and hard to keep for anyone without a door of his own.
A potboy of the district says strangers ask him the way to the grain store and never ask what is done here for the sick.
The watch say strangers ask them where the grain is kept and never ask where the sick are taken.
The guilds of the town say the store a stranger admires was filled by the trades and cannot be opened by them.
The officers of the court say a quarrel over grain is ordinary here and a quarrel over the sick never reaches them.

kept.spine: The law is present here and so is the crime, and neither has the run of the town.

kept.poolKey: First-Survey qualification (the reading is a first look)
kept.spine: The safety of Rundgate is reckoned on a first look, and a first look is honest about what it has seen and silent about what it has not.
Rundgate decides where anything comes in, and the walls and gates are what buy the town that choice.
Some of the soldiers here are hired and the town knows which, and it treats them as hired men.
The trouble a garrison is the wrong tool for goes to the adventurers' guilds here, and they are busy.
A stranger at the gate here is measured in a way he cannot name, and nobody tells him what it was.
The city walls and gates are kept up better than the men who are supposed to stand on them are paid.

kept.poolKey: Logistics & Supply: Granary with road supply
kept.spine: The town keeps a grain store and is fed by the roads, and the store is what stands between a closed road and hunger.
